prize_parts.citation: for discoveries concerning the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms that made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots place B036 first, and I do not treat that as merit in itself. The case rests on the content. The chain runs from proglucagon processing and the identification of the biologically active GLP-1 peptides, through human incretin physiology and glucose-dependent insulin secretion, to central satiety and gastric effects, and then to approved therapies with randomized outcome benefits in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. This is a discernible change in medicine, confirmed independently over more than a decade, with a stable interpretation. A physiology-centred trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov honours the discovery of what the hormone is and does. That fits the prize better than a company-development framing, and it leaves the drug engineering as a recognised downstream consequence rather than the object of the citation.
statement.case_against: The credit is crowded and the three-person limit forces an exclusion. Knudsen's work on long-acting analogues is decisive for the clinical result, and Habener, who is outside the credited names, has a real claim to the early peptide work. My configuration depends on the committee accepting that the prize rewards physiology rather than product development, and on Mojsov's contribution to the active peptide form being weighed fairly against these claims. Priority details are from my recollection and not verified in the supplied evidence.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that the span from basic physiology to the design of liraglutide and semaglutide is the coherent story and that Mojsov's role is contested.
responses.response: I take the point that Knudsen's engineering is what made the therapy real, and I would not call it minor. I still disagree with putting a drug-development contribution in place of the identification of the active peptide. Without the 7-36 form and the physiology, the pharmacology has no target to optimise. Contested credit is not a reason to drop her, because the dispute concerns allocation among discoverers and not whether the contribution was foundational. I could support Knudsen if the committee decides the citation should be therapeutic. I would then want an explicit argument for why that framing is better, since I do not find it persuasive yet.

responses.point: Sandberg also ranks B036 first with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating Mojsov as a real but contested credit that the three-person limit makes difficult to keep.
responses.response: We agree on the science and the maturity, so the difference is only in the third name. Where I would press back is on the idea that the trade-off is symmetrical. Holst and Drucker already carry the physiology and the mechanistic and translational biology. The remaining slot should go to whoever supplies the part of the discovery they do not, which is the identity of the active peptide. I am open to hearing the argument for Knudsen, but I would want it made on discovery grounds and not on the commercial scale of the drugs.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius places TNF blockade (B031) second, as a clear bench-to-bedside discovery that established cytokine blockade as a therapeutic principle across several diseases.
responses.response: This is a strong candidate that I underrated in my own opening, which did not rank it. I accept the clinical breadth. My reservation is attribution. Credit for TNF is spread across those who cloned and characterised the cytokine and those who engineered the antibodies, and the supplied names cover only the synovial and clinical part. I regard it as a serious future candidate, but it is less ready than B036 in terms of a clean allocation, and I would not put it ahead of B042 or B006 on present evidence.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks BCR-ABL inhibition (B026) second, as transformative proof of principle for kinase-directed therapy, with Druker, Lydon and Sawyers as a coherent trio, while noting that the chemistry and earlier oncogene work are outside the credited names.
responses.response: The clinical transformation is beyond dispute and I respect the principle it proved. The gap you flag is the one that concerns me. If the earlier BCR-ABL fusion and oncogene discoveries and the chemistry behind imatinib sit outside the credited names, the trio rewards the development rather than the discovery, and that is the same framing issue I am arguing against for GLP-1. I would be inconsistent if I accepted it here and rejected it there, so I would need the committee to settle that principle first.

responses.point: Perlmann shares the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio, but notes that Habener's absence from the credited names and the place of Knudsen's industrial work are unresolved.
responses.response: We agree on the trio, so my interest is in your caveat. Habener's absence means the committee cannot fully reward the original peptide work from the supplied names, and we should say so openly in the record rather than treat the trio as a complete answer. I would still go ahead with the configuration, since the credited names are what we can name, but I would want that limitation noted when the citation is worded.

uncertainties: Whether the third laureate should be Mojsov or Knudsen, and whether the citation should reward physiology or therapy.
Habener's priority claim sits outside the credited names, so the physiology story may be incompletely represented.

If B036 is set aside, how the committee would weigh optogenetics (B042), with six credited names for three places, against the unfolded protein response (B006), which has a cleaner two-person allocation but less direct clinical effect.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented connections (a 2019 synthesis with Grillner, work with Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons) do not concern any credited name on the shortlist. My field of motor-circuit neuroscience is close to B042 (optogenetics), which I list only as an alternative, and I have no documented involvement with its candidates.
